title: Iceberg Observability in Snowflake Horizon Catalog
summary: See every Iceberg read, write and failed request from Spark, Trino and PyIceberg in Snowflake Horizon Catalog with Access History and event table telemetry.
body_markdown:
An Apache Spark™ job running in another team's environment overwrote a table late last night. This morning, a Trino dashboard is showing different numbers than it did yesterday, and a PyIceberg pipeline is failing with errors nobody can explain. Someone has to answer three questions: who changed the table, what exactly changed and why the pipeline's requests are being rejected.


In most lakehouse architectures, those answers sit in places a data team can't easily reach: catalog server logs, engine-side logs spread across clusters or nowhere at all. Opening your catalog to any engine makes you more agile, but tracking external activity requires unified visibility across all tools.


We have addressed this challenge, and we are excited to review two capabilities for Snowflake Horizon Catalog's Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) APIs: **Access History for Horizon Catalog** and **Horizon Catalog telemetry in Event Tables** . Both features are **generally available** .


External engines' reads and writes now appear in the same ACCESS\\_HISTORY view that audits your Snowflake SQL. HTTP requests made by those engines, including failures, land in your event table. Together, they make Snowflake Horizon Catalog one of the most observable Iceberg REST catalogs in the industry.


## Why observability is the missing half of an open lakehouse


Snowflake Horizon Catalog provides[complete interoperability](https://www.snowflake.com/en/blog/engineering/bidirectional-interoperability-iceberg-snowflake-horizon-catalog/) by allowing teams to[connect Spark, Trino, DuckDB, PyIceberg and other engines](https://www.snowflake.com/en/developers/guides/govern-iceberg-tables-for-external-engines-with-snowflake-horizon/) as needed for their workloads. That flexibility is the point of an open lakehouse.


It also changes who touches your data. Requests that once came only from your warehouse now come from many engines, accounts and service identities. Most catalogs answer "Can this request proceed?" but say far less about what happens afterward. When that record is missing, three things suffer:


- **Audit and compliance:** Security teams can't produce a single, complete record of who read or modified sensitive tables. They have to stitch it together from each engine.
- **Operations:** Platform teams can't see failing or misconfigured clients until a user files a ticket.
- **Trust:** When numbers change, data teams can't trace the change back to the operation, snapshot and identity that caused it.


Horizon Catalog already[governs Apache Iceberg™ tables accessed from external engines](https://www.snowflake.com/en/blog/engineering/unified-governance-iceberg-rest-catalog/) . With this release, it also shows you what those engines are doing.


## Access History and telemetry for Snowflake Horizon Catalog


**Access History for Horizon Catalog** records every successful IRC operation on Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables in the` SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.ACCESS_HISTORY` view. That covers reads such as` loadTable` and metadata fetches; DML such as append, overwrite, delete and truncate; and DDL such as create, alter, drop and rename. These records sit next to the existing records for SQL run in Snowflake and use the same 365-day retention. Access History is available in Enterprise Edition and higher.


**Horizon Catalog telemetry** writes one record to your account's event table for every HTTP request an external engine makes to Horizon Catalog's IRC APIs. Each record captures the request, the identity behind it and the outcome, whether it succeeded or failed.


Figure 1: Architecture diagram. External engines (Spark, Trino, DuckDB, PyIceberg) call Snowflake Horizon Catalog. Successful operations flow to ACCESS_HISTORY. Every request, whether success or failure, flows to the account event table. Both are queried with SQL in Snowflake.


## Three pillars of an observable catalog


### Audit: One access history for every engine


Before this release, an access history that covered only Snowflake SQL told just part of the story. Now you can tell IRC activity apart from Snowflake SQL with one column,` event_source` . Its value is` snowflake_sql` for queries run in Snowflake and` horizon_irc` for calls through the Iceberg REST Catalog.


For IRC events, the` additional_properties` column records which Iceberg operation took place, such as` LoadTable` ,` CreateTable` or` UpdateTable` . Writes include more detail: the kind of change inferred (` append` ,` overwrite` ,` delete` or` truncate` ) and the parent and resulting snapshot IDs. You can tie a change in your data back to the snapshot that introduced it and the Snowflake user that authenticated the engine.


Access History also shows how your governance was applied. When an external engine reads a table protected by a masking or row access policy through the[Scan Plan API](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/tables-iceberg-enforce-access-policies-scan-plan-api) (in public preview), the` policies_referenced` column records which policies Snowflake evaluated for the request and the table and columns they cover. Auditors get evidence that the policies protecting your Snowflake SQL also applied to a Spark job or a PyIceberg script, not just a record that the table was read.


Coming soon, a new` user_agent` field in` additional_properties` will record the client software behind each request, such as` pyiceberg/0.9.0` . You'll be able to break down activity by engine or client as well as by user, and see which client made a given change even when several engines share one service account.


Reads appear in` direct_objects_accessed` and writes appear in` object_modified_by_ddl` . A single query against a fully qualified table name returns everything any external engine has done to that table, including the policies Snowflake evaluated along the way:


```text
SELECT DISTINCT
h.query_start_time,
h.user_name,
h.additional_properties:"irc_event_type"::string AS irc_event_type,
h.additional_properties:"operation"::string      AS operation,
h.policies_referenced
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.ACCESS_HISTORY h,
LATERAL FLATTEN(
ARRAY_CAT(NVL(h.direct_objects_accessed, ARRAY_CONSTRUCT()),
ARRAY_CONSTRUCT(h.object_modified_by_ddl))) f
WHERE h.event_source = 'horizon_irc'
AND h.query_start_time >= DATEADD('day', -90, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
AND f.value:"objectName"::string = 'MY_DB.MY_SCHEMA.ORDERS'
ORDER BY h.query_start_time DESC;
```


Because these records live in the same view as your Snowflake SQL history, existing compliance reports, data-access reviews and security dashboards can cover external engines with little to no extra work.


### Operate: Every request, whether success or failure, in your event table


Access History tells you what happened to your data. Telemetry tells you how your catalog is behaving. After you enable it, each Iceberg REST Catalog request to Horizon Catalog becomes a structured record in your event table. Every record includes:


- **The request:** The HTTP method and route, and the IRC operation, such as` loadTable` ,` updateTable` ,` createTable` ,` dropTable` or` reportMetrics` .
- **The identity:** The Snowflake user that authenticated the client and the roles active for the request.
- **The outcome:** The HTTP response status code.
- **The context:** A unique request ID, plus trace and span IDs for correlation.


Access History records only successful operations. Telemetry also captures requests that fail. That makes it the right tool for problems that never reach your data, such as a misconfigured client, a malformed request or a pipeline using the wrong role. Finding every failed Horizon Catalog request from the last day takes one query:


```text
SELECT observed_timestamp,
record_attributes:"snow.polaris.operation_id"::string   AS operation,
record_attributes:"snow.polaris.principal_name"::string AS principal,
value:"http.response.status_code"::number              AS status_code
FROM my_db.my_schema.my_event_table
WHERE scope:"name"::string = 'snow.managed_polaris'
AND value:"http.response.status_code"::number >= 400
AND observed_timestamp >= DATEADD('day', -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
ORDER BY observed_timestamp DESC;
```


Figure 2: Screenshot of the query results in the Snowsight interface, showing failed requests by operation and principal.


### Act: Your own observability data you can build on


These records live in Snowflake tables, not in a separate logging system. You work with them using the tools you already have in order to:


- **Alert** on spikes in failed requests or unexpected write activity with Snowflake alerts.
- **Visualize IRC traffic by user, operation and table** with Snowsight dashboards.
- **Correlate** telemetry with Access History and query history to follow an incident from a failing request to the data it affected.
- **Govern** the observability data itself with the same roles and policies that protect the rest of your account.


There are no agents to deploy, no log pipelines to maintain and no extra infrastructure to run.


## What makes Snowflake Horizon Catalog one of the most observable catalogs


Observability for an open catalog should mean more than just having logs somewhere. With this release, Horizon Catalog gives you:


- **Complete operation coverage:** Reads, DML and DDL from any engine are recorded in Access History.
- **Failures as well as successes:** HTTP requests, including the rejected ones, are recorded in telemetry.
- **Identity on every record:** You see the authenticated user and active roles, not just an IP address or client ID.
- **Proof of enforcement:** Access History records which masking and row access policies Snowflake evaluated for each external-engine request.
- **Snapshot-level change tracking:** Each write records the operation type and the snapshot IDs it produced.
- **One audit plane:** External-engine activity sits in the same ACCESS\\_HISTORY view as Snowflake SQL, with the same retention.
- **SQL-native analysis:** Everything is queryable, joinable and governable in Snowflake, with nothing extra to deploy.


Openness and visibility are often treated as a trade-off. With Horizon Catalog, you get both.


## Get started


1. **Explore Access History:** Query` SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.ACCESS_HISTORY` with` event_source = 'horizon_irc'` to see external-engine activity on your Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables.[Docs: Horizon Catalog operations in ACCESS\\_HISTORY](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/tables-iceberg-access-using-external-query-engine-snowflake-horizon-access-history)
2. **Turn on telemetry:** Make sure your account has an event table, and set` LOG_LEVEL` to at least` INFO` .[Docs: Capture Horizon Catalog events in the event table](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/tables-iceberg-access-using-external-query-engine-snowflake-horizon-telemetry)
3. **Connect an engine:** If you aren't using Horizon Catalog with external engines yet, connect Spark, Trino, DuckDB or PyIceberg to your Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables.[Docs: Access Iceberg tables with an external engine through Horizon Catalog](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/externally-managed-iceberg-tables-access-horizon-irc)
